document:
Overview > Patterns

**Graph execution**

    Visualize multi-step graph pipelines with per-node status and streaming content.
  
  **Custom stream channels**

    Stream custom server-side data to the frontend and read it with `useExtension` and `useChannel`.

Overview > Related patterns

The [LangChain frontend patterns](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/frontend/overview)—markdown messages, tool calling, human-in-the-loop, resumable streams, and time travel—work with any LangGraph graph. The stream API provides the same core data model whether you use `createAgent`, `createDeepAgent`, or a custom `StateGraph`.

Functional API overview
Wrap other frameworks with entrypoints and tasks for LangSmith Agent Server. Covers checkpointing, resume rules, and common pitfalls.

The **Functional API** wraps ordinary functions with LangGraph runtime features ([persistence](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence), [memory](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/add-memory), [human-in-the-loop](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts), and [streaming](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming)). Use it when you already have existing code or are using a different framework and want to [deploy it on LangSmith](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/deploy-other-frameworks) without rewriting that agent as a graph. Prefer the [Graph API](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api) for building new agents.

This page is the concept reference for entrypoints, tasks, checkpointing, and resume rules. For the wrap-and-deploy how-to, see [Deploy other frameworks](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/deploy-other-frameworks).

The Functional API uses two building blocks:

* **`@entrypoint`**: Marks a function as the start of a workflow. It manages execution, interrupts, and checkpointing.
* **`@task`**: Marks a discrete unit of work (for example, an API call). Tasks return a future-like object that you can await or resolve with `.result()`.

Functional API overview > When to use the Functional API

| Build | Use |
| --- | --- |
| New LangGraph agents and workflows | [Graph API](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api) |
| Existing agent in another framework (Claude Agent SDK, Strands, CrewAI, AutoGen, and similar) that you want on LangSmith Agent Server | Functional API via [Deploy other frameworks](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/deploy-other-frameworks) |

Compared with the Graph API, the Functional API uses ordinary language control flow (`if` / `else`, loops, and calls), keeps values scoped to the entrypoint and tasks instead of a shared [state](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#state) schema, saves task results on the entrypoint checkpoint rather than after each [super-step](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#super-steps), and has no static graph visualization.

document:
Functional API overview > Entrypoint

The `@entrypoint` decorator creates a workflow from a function. It manages long-running work and [interrupts](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts).

Functional API overview > Entrypoint > Definition

Pass a [checkpointer](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence) when you need persistence or human-in-the-loop. Identify each run with a `thread_id` in config. A thread is the durable identity for one conversation or workflow run.

An **entrypoint** is a function decorated with `@entrypoint`.

The function **must accept a single positional argument** as the workflow input. To pass multiple values, use a dictionary (or similar) as that argument.

Decorating the function produces a workflow object (a @[`Pregel`][Pregel.stream] instance). Call `invoke` or `ainvoke` to run it.

    **Sync**

    
    
    **Async**

    
    

**Warning:** 
**Serialization**
Entrypoint **inputs** and **outputs** must be JSON-serializable when a checkpointer is configured. See [Serialization](#serialization).

Functional API overview > Entrypoint > Run and resume

Call `invoke` or `ainvoke` for a final result. For streams, see [Streaming](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming).

Resume after @[`interrupt`] by passing a resume value in @[`Command`]. For recipes, see [Interrupts](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts).

After an error, resume the same `thread_id` with `None`.

Functional API overview > Entrypoint > Short-term memory

When an `entrypoint` has a `checkpointer`, successive invocations on the same **thread id** store state in [checkpoints](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/checkpointers#checkpoints).

Add a keyword-only `previous` parameter. LangGraph sets it to the last value saved on this thread. On the first run it is `None`. To save a different value for the next run, use @[`entrypoint.final`][entrypoint.final].

Functional API overview > Entrypoint > Injectable parameters

You can skip this until you add [memory](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/add-memory) or [custom streaming](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming).

When declaring an `entrypoint`, you can request additional parameters that LangGraph injects at runtime:

| Parameter | Description |
| --------- | ----------- |
| **previous** | The return value from the previous invocation on the same thread (requires a checkpointer). See [short-term memory](#short-term-memory). |
| **config** | A @[`RunnableConfig`] object with run-time configuration values. |
| **store** | A @[`BaseStore`] instance for [long-term memory](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/add-memory). Also available as `runtime.store`. |
| **writer** | A `StreamWriter` for custom streaming. Also available as `runtime.stream_writer`. See [Streaming](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming). |
| **runtime** | A @[`Runtime`] object for the current run, including context, store, and writer. |

**Warning:** 
Declare injectable parameters with the appropriate name and type annotation.

**Requesting injectable parameters**

Functional API overview > Task

A **task** is a discrete unit of work (for example, an API call or data step). Tasks have two key properties:

* **Concurrent execution**: Calling a task starts it immediately. The entrypoint blocks only when you wait for the result, so independent tasks can overlap.
* **Checkpointing**: Task results are saved so resume can restore them. See [persistence](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence).

Functional API overview > Task > Definition

Define tasks with the `@task` decorator:

**Warning:** 
**Serialization**: Task **outputs** must be JSON-serializable to support checkpointing.

Functional API overview > Task > Execution

Call **tasks** only from an **entrypoint**, another **task**, or a [Graph API node](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#nodes). Do not call them from application code outside the workflow.

Calling a task returns a future immediately. Resolve it with `.result()` (sync) or `await` (async).

    **Sync**

    
    
    **Async**

Functional API overview > Task > When to use a task

Use **tasks** when you need:

* **Checkpointing**: Save a long-running result so resume does not recompute it.
* **Human-in-the-loop**: Wrap work you should not redo after a pause in a task, for example an LLM call. Resume after an [interrupt](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts) restores the result. For randomness, see [Determinism](#determinism).
* **Parallel execution**: Run independent I/O-bound work concurrently.
* **Observability**: Track discrete steps in [LangSmith](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability).
* **Retries**: Apply retry policies to discrete units of work. See [Fault tolerance](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance).

document:
Functional API overview > Resume and checkpointing

Resume replay depends on serialization, determinism, and idempotency.

Functional API overview > Resume and checkpointing > Serialization

Two rules apply when a checkpointer is configured:

1. `entrypoint` inputs and outputs must be JSON-serializable.
2. `task` outputs must be JSON-serializable.

Use Python primitives such as dictionaries, lists, strings, numbers, and booleans.

Serialization is what makes task results and intermediate values restorable for human-in-the-loop, fault tolerance, and parallel execution. Non-serializable values raise a runtime error when a checkpointer is configured.

Functional API overview > Resume and checkpointing > Determinism

Resume does **not** continue from the exact line where execution stopped. Execution returns to a checkpoint boundary and **replays** forward until it hits the pause again.

For the Functional API, replay starts at the beginning of the **entrypoint**. LangGraph restores completed [**task**](#task) and [**subgraph**](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/use-subgraphs) results from the checkpointer instead of recomputing them. That preserves step order across pauses, including for long-running or non-deterministic **task** outputs.

For **human-in-the-loop**, put non-deterministic work (for example, random values) and side effects (for example, file writes or API calls) in [**tasks**](#task).

Different runs can produce different results. Resuming a **specific** thread should replay the same persisted **task** and **subgraph** results.

Guidelines:

* **Avoid repeating work**: Give each side effect in an entrypoint its own **task** so resume restores outputs instead of re-running them.
* **Encapsulate non-deterministic operations**: Keep values that change between attempts (random numbers, wall-clock time) inside **tasks**.
* **Use idempotent operations**: For partial failures and retries, see [Idempotency](#idempotency).

Functional API overview > Resume and checkpointing > Idempotency

Idempotency means running the same operation more than once has the same effect as running it once. Place API calls and other writes inside **tasks**, and design those tasks to be safe if they run again.

On resume, LangGraph restores completed **task** results. A **task** that started but did not finish may run again, so use idempotency keys or check existing results before writing.

Functional API overview > Pause for human review

This workflow writes an essay and [interrupts](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts) for human review:

Invoke with a topic such as `"cat"`. The run writes the essay, then pauses at `interrupt`. The pause can last indefinitely. Resume starts at the beginning of the entrypoint.

The `write_essay` task result is restored, not recomputed.

For stream, resume, and tool-call review, see [Interrupts](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts).

Functional API overview > Common pitfalls > Handling side effects

Put side effects (writing a file, sending an email) in tasks so resume does not run them again.

    **Incorrect**

    The file write runs in the entrypoint, so resume executes it a second time.

    ```python
    from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver
    from langgraph.func import entrypoint
    from langgraph.types import interrupt

    checkpointer = InMemorySaver()

    @entrypoint(checkpointer=checkpointer)
    def my_workflow(inputs: dict) -> int:
        # Runs again on resume.
        with open("output.txt", "w") as f:
            f.write("Side effect executed")
        value = interrupt("question")
        return value
    ```

    
    **Correct**

    The side effect lives in a task, so resume restores the checkpointed result.

    ```python
    from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver
    from langgraph.func import entrypoint, task
    from langgraph.types import interrupt

    checkpointer = InMemorySaver()

    @task
    def write_to_file() -> None:
        with open("output.txt", "w") as f:
            f.write("Side effect executed")

    @entrypoint(checkpointer=checkpointer)
    def my_workflow(inputs: dict) -> int:
        write_to_file().result()
        value = interrupt("question")
        return value
    ```

Functional API overview > Learn more

- [Deploy other frameworks](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/deploy-other-frameworks)
- [Graph API overview](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api)
- [Interrupts](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts)
- [Streaming](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming)
- [Fault tolerance](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance)
- [Memory](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/add-memory)

Build sequences, branches, and loops
Compose sequences, parallel branches, conditional edges, and loops with the LangGraph Graph API.

Compose [sequences](#create-a-sequence-of-steps), [parallel branches](#create-branches), [conditional edges](#conditional-branching), and [loops](#create-and-control-loops) with the Graph API. For map-reduce fan-out and returning edges from nodes, see [Use Send and Command](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-send-command). For node-level retries, timeouts, and caching, see [Configure nodes](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-nodes).

Build sequences, branches, and loops > Create a sequence of steps

**Info:** 
**Prerequisites**
This guide assumes familiarity with [Define and update state](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state).

This section shows how to build a sequential graph. Python also has an `add_sequence` shorthand for the same pattern.

```mermaid
%%{init:{'theme':'base','themeVariables':{'lineColor':'#40668D','primaryColor':'#E5F4FF','primaryTextColor':'#030710','primaryBorderColor':'#006DDD'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    startNode([START]) --> s1[step_1]
    s1 --> s2[step_2]
    s2 --> s3[step_3]

    classDef process fill:#E5F4FF,stroke:#006DDD,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    classDef terminal fill:#F2FAFF,stroke:#40668D,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710

```

Add a sequence of nodes with @[`add_node`] and @[`add_edge`] on a [StateGraph](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#stategraph):

Or use the built-in shorthand `.add_sequence`:

**Why split application steps into a sequence with LangGraph?**

LangGraph can add a persistence layer under the graph. State is checkpointed between nodes, so those nodes govern:

* How state updates are [checkpointed](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence)
* How interruptions resume in [human-in-the-loop](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts) workflows
* How to rewind and branch executions with [time travel](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/use-time-travel)

They also shape how steps are [streamed](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming), and how the app is visualized and debugged in [Studio](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/studio).

The following end-to-end example builds a sequence of three steps:

1. Populate a value in a key of the state
2. Update the same value
3. Populate a different value

First define the [state](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#state). For how updates merge, see [Process state updates with reducers](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state#process-state-updates-with-reducers).

This example tracks two values:

[Nodes](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#nodes) are Python functions that read graph state and return updates. The first argument is always the state:

**Note:** 
Each node update can name only the keys it changes.

By default, that **overwrites** the previous value for those keys. Use [reducers](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#reducers) when updates should append or combine instead. See [Process state updates with reducers](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state#process-state-updates-with-reducers).

Next, define a [StateGraph](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#stategraph) on that state and wire the nodes.

Use [`add_node`](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#nodes) and [`add_edge`](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#edges) to populate the graph and define its control flow.

**Tip:** 
**Specifying custom names**
Pass an explicit name as the first argument to @[`add_node`]:

Note that:

Build sequences, branches, and loops > Create a sequence of steps

* @[`add_edge`] takes node names. For bare functions, the default name is `node.__name__`.
* The graph needs an entry point: add an edge from the [START node](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#start-node).
* The graph halts when there are no more nodes to execute.

Then [compile](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#compiling-your-graph) the graph. Compile runs basic structure checks (for example, orphaned nodes). Pass a [checkpointer](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence) here when the app needs persistence.

Invoke the graph:

```
{'value_1': 'a b', 'value_2': 10}
```

Note that:

* This invoke passes a value for one state key. Nodes can also write keys that were not in the input.
* The first node overwrites the value that was passed in.
* The second node updates that value.
* The third node populates a different key.

**Tip:** 
**Built-in shorthand**
`langgraph>=0.2.46` includes a built-in short-hand `add_sequence` for adding node sequences. You can compile the same graph as follows:

Build sequences, branches, and loops > Create branches

Parallel node execution speeds up graph runs. LangGraph fans out and fans in with standard edges and @[conditional_edges][add_conditional_edges]. The following examples build branching dataflows. For map-reduce fan-out to dynamic targets, see [Use Send and Command](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-send-command).

Build sequences, branches, and loops > Create branches > Run graph nodes in parallel

This example fans out from `Node A` to `B` and `C`, then fans in to `D`. The state uses a [reducer](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#reducers) so values accumulate for that key instead of overwriting. For lists, that means concatenating the new list onto the existing list. See [Process state updates with reducers](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state#process-state-updates-with-reducers).

```mermaid
%%{init:{'theme':'base','themeVariables':{'lineColor':'#40668D','primaryColor':'#E5F4FF','primaryTextColor':'#030710','primaryBorderColor':'#006DDD'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    startNode([START]) --> a[a]
    a --> b[b]
    a --> c[c]
    b --> d[d]
    c --> d
    d --> endNode([END])

    classDef process fill:#E5F4FF,stroke:#006DDD,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    classDef terminal fill:#F2FAFF,stroke:#40668D,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    class a,b,c,d process
    class startNode,endNode terminal
```

With the reducer, you can see that the values added in each node are accumulated.

```
Adding "A" to []
Adding "B" to ['A']
Adding "C" to ['A']
Adding "D" to ['A', 'B', 'C']
```

**Note:** 
In the above example, nodes `"b"` and `"c"` are executed concurrently in the same [superstep](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#super-steps). Because they are in the same step, node `"d"` executes after both `"b"` and `"c"` are finished.

Importantly, updates from a parallel superstep may not be ordered consistently. If you need a consistent, predetermined ordering of updates from a parallel superstep, you should write the outputs to a separate field in the state together with a value with which to order them.

**Exception handling**

  LangGraph runs nodes in [supersteps](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#super-steps). Parallel branches in a superstep run concurrently, but the superstep is **transactional**: if any branch raises, **none** of that superstep's updates apply to state.

  With a [checkpointer](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence), results from successful nodes in a completed superstep are saved and do not repeat when the run resumes.

  For flaky work such as unreliable API calls, use either:

  1. Ordinary `try` / `except` (or equivalent) inside the node.
  2. A **[`RetryPolicy`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/types/#langgraph.types.RetryPolicy)** on the node so LangGraph retries selected exceptions. Only failing branches retry, so successful siblings are not re-run.

  Together, these keep parallel execution while you control how failures are handled. For a full guide, see [Fault tolerance](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance).

**Tip:** 
**Set max concurrency**
Pass `max_concurrency` as a top-level config key (not under `configurable`) when invoking the graph. See [RunnableConfig](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langchain-core/runnables/config/RunnableConfig).

document:
Build sequences, branches, and loops > Create branches > Defer node execution

Deferring node execution delays a node until all other pending tasks are completed. This matters when branches have different lengths, which is common in map-reduce workflows.

The parallel example above fans out and fans in when each path is one step. Add a node `"b_2"` on the `"b"` branch so the paths have unequal length. Node `d` uses `defer` so it waits for the longer branch:

```mermaid
%%{init:{'theme':'base','themeVariables':{'lineColor':'#40668D','primaryColor':'#E5F4FF','primaryTextColor':'#030710','primaryBorderColor':'#006DDD'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    startNode([START]) --> a[a]
    a --> b[b]
    a --> c[c]
    b --> b2[b_2]
    b2 --> d[d]
    c --> d
    d --> endNode([END])

    classDef process fill:#E5F4FF,stroke:#006DDD,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    classDef terminal fill:#F2FAFF,stroke:#40668D,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    class a,b,b2,c,d process
    class startNode,endNode terminal
```

```
Adding "A" to []
Adding "B" to ['A']
Adding "C" to ['A']
Adding "B_2" to ['A', 'B', 'C']
Adding "D" to ['A', 'B', 'C', 'B_2']
```

Nodes `"b"` and `"c"` run concurrently in the same superstep. `defer=True` on node `d` keeps it from running until all pending tasks finish, so `"d"` waits for the full `"b"` branch.

When every branch always runs, you can wait with a list-form edge instead of `defer=True`. `add_edge` also accepts a list of start nodes. This is not shorthand for separate `add_edge` calls; the two forms behave differently:

- **A list of start nodes** runs `d` once, after all of the listed nodes have completed. If one of them never runs (for example, a conditional edge does not select its branch), `d` never runs and no error is raised. State updates from branches that did complete remain in the graph state, but `d` does not consume them.
- **Separate edges** run `d` once per superstep in which any incoming branch completes. With branches of equal length, that is a single run; with branches of different lengths, `d` runs more than once.
- **Separate edges with `defer=True`** (the pattern in the example above) run `d` once, after every selected branch has completed, whether the fan-out selected all of the branches or only some of them.

`defer=True` postpones the node until no tasks are pending anywhere in the graph, not only in the branches that feed it. A [`Send`](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-send-command) addressed to the node still invokes it separately.

Build sequences, branches, and loops > Create branches > Conditional branching

Route to different nodes at runtime from state. Node `a` updates state, then a conditional edge chooses `b` or `c`:

```mermaid
%%{init:{'theme':'base','themeVariables':{'lineColor':'#40668D','primaryColor':'#E5F4FF','primaryTextColor':'#030710','primaryBorderColor':'#006DDD'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    startNode([START]) --> a[a]
    a -.-> b[b]
    a -.-> c[c]
    b --> endNode([END])
    c --> endNode

    classDef process fill:#E5F4FF,stroke:#006DDD,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    classDef terminal fill:#F2FAFF,stroke:#40668D,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    class a,b,c process
    class startNode,endNode terminal
```

Dashed edges are conditional routes.

If your fan-out should vary at runtime based on the state, you can use @[`add_conditional_edges`] to select one or more paths using the graph state. See the following example, where node `a` generates a state update that determines the next node.

```
Adding "A" to []
Adding "C" to ['A']
{'aggregate': ['A', 'C'], 'which': 'c'}
```

**Tip:** 
Your conditional edges can route to multiple destination nodes. For example:

Build sequences, branches, and loops > Create and control loops

A loop needs a way to stop. The usual pattern is a [conditional edge](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#conditional-edges) that routes to [END](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#end-node) when a termination condition is met.

You can also set a recursion limit when invoking or streaming. The limit is the number of [super-steps](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#super-steps) allowed before LangGraph raises an error. See the [recursion limit concept](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#recursion-limit).

The following examples use a simple looping graph. Node `a` either continues to `b` (which returns to `a`) or exits:

```mermaid
%%{init:{'theme':'base','themeVariables':{'lineColor':'#40668D','primaryColor':'#E5F4FF','primaryTextColor':'#030710','primaryBorderColor':'#006DDD'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    startNode([START]) --> a[a]
    a -.-> b[b]
    a -.-> endNode([END])
    b --> a

    classDef process fill:#E5F4FF,stroke:#006DDD,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    classDef terminal fill:#F2FAFF,stroke:#40668D,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    class a,b process
    class startNode,endNode terminal
```

Dashed edges are conditional routes.

**Tip:** 
To catch `GraphRecursionError` after the limit is hit, see [Impose a recursion limit](#impose-a-recursion-limit). To route to a completion path before the limit, see [Handle recursion with RemainingSteps](#handle-recursion-with-remainingsteps).

Add a conditional edge that encodes the termination condition:

To control the recursion limit, specify `"recursion_limit"` in the config. This will raise a `GraphRecursionError`, which you can catch and handle:

Define a graph with a simple loop. A conditional edge implements the termination condition.

This architecture is similar to a [ReAct agent](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/workflows-agents) in which node `"a"` is a tool-calling model, and node `"b"` represents the tools.

The `route` conditional edge ends the run after the `"aggregate"` list passes a threshold length.

When you invoke the graph, it alternates between nodes `"a"` and `"b"` until that condition is met.

```
Node A sees []
Node B sees ['A']
Node A sees ['A', 'B']
Node B sees ['A', 'B', 'A']
Node A sees ['A', 'B', 'A', 'B']
Node B sees ['A', 'B', 'A', 'B', 'A']
Node A sees ['A', 'B', 'A', 'B', 'A', 'B']
```

Build sequences, branches, and loops > Create and control loops > Impose a recursion limit

When a termination condition is not guaranteed, set the graph's [recursion limit](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#recursion-limit). LangGraph raises `GraphRecursionError` after that many [supersteps](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#super-steps). Catch and handle the exception:

```
Node A sees []
Node B sees ['A']
Node A sees ['A', 'B']
Node B sees ['A', 'B', 'A']
Node A sees ['A', 'B', 'A', 'B']
Recursion Error
```

**Extended example: loops with branches**

A more complex loop fans out one step into two nodes:

```mermaid
%%{init:{'theme':'base','themeVariables':{'lineColor':'#40668D','primaryColor':'#E5F4FF','primaryTextColor':'#030710','primaryBorderColor':'#006DDD'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    startNode([START]) --> a[a]
    a -.-> b[b]
    a -.-> endNode([END])
    b --> c[c]
    b --> d[d]
    c --> a
    d --> a

    classDef process fill:#E5F4FF,stroke:#006DDD,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    classDef terminal fill:#F2FAFF,stroke:#40668D,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    class a,b,c,d process
    class startNode,endNode terminal
```

Dashed edges are conditional routes from `a`.

This graph is a loop of [supersteps](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#super-steps): Node A, then B, then C and D concurrent, then back to A. The list-form edge waits for both `"c"` and `"d"` before returning to `"a"`. For how list-form edges differ from separate edges into the same node, see [Defer node execution](#defer-node-execution).

Invoking without a recursion limit completes two full laps before the termination condition:

```
Node A sees []
Node B sees ['A']
Node D sees ['A', 'B']
Node C sees ['A', 'B']
Node A sees ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']
Node B sees ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'A']
Node D sees ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'A', 'B']
Node C sees ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'A', 'B']
Node A sees ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'A', 'B', 'C', 'D']
```

With the recursion limit set to four, only one lap completes because each lap is four supersteps:

```
Node A sees []
Node B sees ['A']
Node C sees ['A', 'B']
Node D sees ['A', 'B']
Node A sees ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']
Recursion Error
```

metadata.section: Create and control loops > Impose a recursion limit

document:
Build sequences, branches, and loops > Create and control loops > Access and handle the recursion counter

Nodes can read the current step from run metadata. Use that to react before the limit is hit.

#### Handle recursion with RemainingSteps

`RemainingSteps` is a Python-only managed value for how many steps remain before the recursion limit. Use it to route to a completion path before LangGraph raises `GraphRecursionError`:

Handle the limit inside the graph with `RemainingSteps`, or catch `GraphRecursionError` outside the graph:

| Approach | Detection | Handling | Control flow |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Proactive (`RemainingSteps`) | Before the limit | Inside the graph via conditional routing | Graph continues to a completion path |
| Reactive (`GraphRecursionError`) | After the limit | Outside the graph in `try` / `except` | Graph execution stops |

Related metadata keys include `langgraph_node`, `langgraph_triggers`, `langgraph_path`, and `langgraph_checkpoint_ns`.

document:
Build sequences, branches, and loops > Async

Async helps when [IO-bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I/O_bound) work can run concurrently. To convert a sync graph to async:

1. Define nodes with `async def` instead of `def`.
2. Use `await` for async calls inside those nodes.
3. Invoke with `.ainvoke` or `.astream`.

Many LangChain objects implement the @[Runnable] protocol, which has async variants of the sync methods. See the [streaming guide](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming) for async streaming examples.

Build sequences, branches, and loops > See also

- [Graph API overview](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api)
- [Use Send and Command](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-send-command)
- [Configure nodes](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-nodes)
- [Visualize your graph](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-visualize)
- [Streaming](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming)

Configure nodes
Add runtime configuration, retry policies, timeouts, error handling, defaults, and caching to LangGraph nodes.

[Nodes](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#nodes) are the steps of a Graph API graph. This page covers how to attach runtime configuration, retries, timeouts, error handlers, defaults, and caching when you add a node. For wiring nodes into sequences, branches, and loops, see [Control flow](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-control-flow). For the full retry, timeout, and error lifecycle, see [Fault tolerance](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance).

Configure nodes > Add runtime configuration

Pass values into a run (for example, which LLM or system prompt to use) without putting those values in graph state.

To add runtime configuration:

1. Specify a schema for your configuration
2. Add the configuration to the function signature for nodes or conditional edges
3. Pass the configuration into the graph

See below for a simple example:

```
{'my_state_value': 1}
{'my_state_value': 2}
```

**Extended example: specifying LLM at runtime**

  Choose OpenAI or Anthropic at invoke time. These examples call live providers and need API keys.

  

  ```
  claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
  gpt-5.4-mini
  ```

**Extended example: specifying model and system message at runtime**

  Configure both the model provider and a system message at invoke time. These examples call live providers and need API keys.

  

  ```
  ================================ Human Message ================================

  hi
  ================================== Ai Message ==================================

  Ciao! Come posso aiutarti oggi?
  ```

Configure nodes > Add retry policies

Attach a retry policy when a node calls an API, database, or LLM that can fail transiently.

Pass `retry_policy` to @[`add_node`]. The value is a `RetryPolicy` named tuple. This example uses the defaults:

By default, `retry_on` uses `default_retry_on`, which retries any exception except:

* `ValueError`
* `TypeError`
* `ArithmeticError`
* `ImportError`
* `LookupError`
* `NameError`
* `SyntaxError`
* `RuntimeError`
* `ReferenceError`
* `StopIteration`
* `StopAsyncIteration`
* `OSError`

For exceptions from popular HTTP libraries such as `requests` and `httpx`, it only retries on 5xx status codes. See [Fault tolerance](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance#retries) for the full default list and parameters.

**Extended example: customizing retry policies**

  These snippets show how to attach different retry policies. They do not create database tables or invoke the graph.

  Pass different retry policies to a model node and a SQL node:

Configure nodes > Set node timeouts

**Note:** 
Requires `langgraph>=1.2`.

Pass `timeout` to @[`add_node`] to cap how long a single async node attempt may run. Use a number (seconds), a `datetime.timedelta`, or a @[`TimeoutPolicy`] for separate run and idle limits:

Node timeouts apply only to **async** nodes. Setting `timeout` on a sync node fails at compile time, because sync Python execution cannot be safely canceled in-process. For separate run and idle limits, pass a @[`TimeoutPolicy`].

When a node exceeds its timeout, LangGraph raises @[`NodeTimeoutError`]. It does **not** subclass built-in `TimeoutError` (an `OSError` subclass), so the default retry policy treats it as retryable when a `retry_policy` is set. The timeout applies to each attempt independently, so the timer resets for every retry. Timed-out attempts do not commit buffered writes.

See [Fault tolerance](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance#timeouts) for the full timeout lifecycle, idle-timeout refresh sources, and `runtime.heartbeat()`.

Configure nodes > Handle node errors

**Note:** 
Requires `langgraph>=1.2`.

Pass `error_handler` to @[`add_node`] to run a function after a node fails and all retries are exhausted. The handler receives the current state and a typed @[`NodeError`], and can route to a recovery branch via @[`Command`]:

See [Fault tolerance](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance#error-handling) for a full runnable example, compensation patterns, and `Command` routing.

Configure nodes > Set graph-wide node defaults

**Note:** 
Requires `langgraph>=1.2`.

Use @[`set_node_defaults`] to set `retry_policy`, `timeout`, `cache_policy`, or `error_handler` once for every node in a graph, instead of repeating them on each @[`add_node`] call. Per-node values always win, and defaults are applied at @[`StateGraph.compile`] time:

`retry_policy` and `timeout` defaults apply to every node, including error-handler nodes. `cache_policy` and `error_handler` defaults apply only to regular nodes—handlers never catch themselves, and caching a handler result is unsafe. Defaults are not inherited by subgraphs.

See [Fault tolerance](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance#graph-defaults) for the full precedence rules and applicability table.

Configure nodes > Access execution info inside a node

Access execution identity and retry information via `runtime.execution_info`. This surfaces thread, run, and checkpoint identifiers as well as retry state, without reading from `config` directly.

| Attribute | Type | Description |
| --------- | ---- | ----------- |
| `thread_id` | `str \| None` | Thread ID for the current execution. `None` without a checkpointer. |
| `run_id` | `str \| None` | Run ID for the current execution. `None` when not provided in config. |
| `checkpoint_id` | `str` | Checkpoint ID for the current execution. |
| `checkpoint_ns` | `str` | Checkpoint namespace for the current execution. |
| `task_id` | `str` | Task ID for the current execution. |
| `node_attempt` | `int` | Current execution attempt number (1-indexed). `1` on the first try, `2` on the first retry, etc. |
| `node_first_attempt_time` | `float \| None` | Unix timestamp (seconds) of when the first attempt started. Stays the same across retries. |

#### Access thread and run IDs

Use `execution_info` to access the thread ID, run ID, and other identity fields inside a node:

#### Adjust behavior based on retry state

When a node has a retry policy, use `execution_info` to inspect the current attempt number and switch to a fallback after the first attempt fails:

`execution_info` is set once the node task is prepared. Even without a retry policy, `node_attempt` defaults to `1`, and `node_first_attempt_time` is set when the node starts executing.

Configure nodes > Access server info inside a node

When your graph runs on LangSmith Agent Server, you can access server-specific metadata via `runtime.server_info`. This surfaces the assistant ID, graph ID, and authenticated user without reading config metadata or configurable keys directly.

| Attribute | Type | Description |
| --------- | ---- | ----------- |
| `assistant_id` | `str` | The assistant ID for the current deployment. |
| `graph_id` | `str` | The graph ID for the current deployment. |
| `user` | `BaseUser \| None` | The authenticated user, if [custom auth](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/custom-auth) is configured. |

`server_info` is `None` when the graph is not running on Agent Server (for example, during local development or testing).

**Note:** 
Requires `langgraph>=1.1.5`.

document:
Configure nodes > Access drain state inside a node

When a [graceful shutdown](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance#graceful-shutdown) has been requested, `runtime.drain_requested` is `True`. Read this inside a node to skip expensive work before the next superstep boundary:

| Property | Type | Description |
| -------- | ---- | ----------- |
| `drain_requested` | `bool` | `True` if `RunControl.request_drain()` has been called for this run. |
| `drain_reason` | `str \| None` | The reason string passed to `request_drain()`, or `None` if drain was not requested. |

**Note:** 
Requires `langgraph>=1.2`. See [Graceful shutdown](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance#graceful-shutdown) for the full `RunControl` API.

document:
Configure nodes > Add node caching

Use node caching when a step is expensive and you want to reuse results for the same input.

To enable caching:

1. Pass a cache when you compile the graph (for example, `InMemoryCache`). `SqliteCache` is also available in Python.
2. Attach a @[`CachePolicy`] on the node.

@[`CachePolicy`] options:

- **`key_func`**: Function that builds a cache key from the node input. Defaults to a hash of the input (via pickle).
- **`ttl`**: Time to live in seconds. When omitted, the cache entry does not expire.

The first run takes about two seconds because of the mocked work. The second run returns from the cache.

You can also set `cache_policy` (and other node options) once for the graph with @[`set_node_defaults`]. See [Set graph-wide node defaults](#set-graph-wide-node-defaults).

Configure nodes > See also

- [Graph API](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#nodes)
- [Control flow](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-control-flow)
- [Fault tolerance](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance)
- [Define and update state](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state)

Use Send and Command
Build map-reduce workflows with Send and combine state updates with routing using Command in LangGraph.

@[`Send`] runs the same node once per item with a custom input when the item count is known only at runtime (map-reduce). @[`Command`] updates state and chooses the next node in one return. For ordinary sequences, branches, and loops, see [Control flow](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-control-flow). For concepts, see [Send](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#send) and [Command](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#command) on the Graph API overview.

Use Send and Command > Use Send for map-reduce

Return one or more `Send` objects from a [conditional edge](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#conditional-edges). Each `Send` names a target node and passes that invocation's input. LangGraph runs those invocations in parallel. When workers write the same state key, use a [reducer](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#reducers) so updates merge (for example, concatenating lists).

The worker below does not receive the full graph state. `Send` passes `{ "subject": ... }` as that run's input, so the worker schema includes `subject` even though the overall state does not.

```python
from IPython.display import Image, display
```

Return `Command(update=...)` from a tool to write graph state (for example, customer lookup results) during a turn. The fragment below assumes `get_user_info` / `getUserInfo` and a message history key named `messages`. Complete the imports and helpers in your app.

Use Send and Command > Resume after an interrupt

Use `Command` as input to `invoke` / `stream` only to resume after an [interrupt](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts) (`resume=...`, optionally with `update` while resuming). Do not pass `Command(update=...)` alone to continue a conversation: any `Command` as input resumes from the latest checkpoint, not from `START`. Pass a plain state update to start a new turn.

For the full anti-pattern example, see [Input to invoke or stream](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#input-to-invoke-or-stream). For interrupt patterns, see [Interrupts](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts).

Use Send and Command > See also

- [Send](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#send) and [Command](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#command) on the Graph API overview
- [Interrupts](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts)
- [Control flow](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-control-flow)
- [Use subgraphs](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/use-subgraphs)
- [Configure nodes](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-nodes)

Define and update state
Define graph state schemas, reducers, messages, and private state in the LangGraph Graph API.

[State](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#state) is the shared schema that nodes read and write. [Reducers](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#reducers) control how each update merges into the current value. This page covers:

1. How to use state to define a graph's [schema](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#schema)
2. How to use reducers to control how state updates are processed

Define and update state > Define state

[State](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#state) in LangGraph can be a `TypedDict`, `Pydantic` model, or dataclass. The examples below use `TypedDict`. Prefer that form for most graphs; see [Use Pydantic models for graph state](#use-pydantic-models-for-graph-state) when you need runtime validation on inputs.

By default, a graph uses the same schema for input and output, and the state determines that schema. See [Define input and output schemas](#define-input-and-output-schemas) for distinct input and output schemas.

Start with a [messages](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#working-with-messages-in-graph-state) field. That shape fits many LLM applications. For more detail, see [Working with messages in graph state](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#working-with-messages-in-graph-state).

This state tracks a list of [message](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/messages) objects and an extra integer field. There is no reducer yet, so a node that updates `messages` must return the full list.

Define and update state > Update state

Build a graph with a single [node](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#nodes). The node is a Python function that reads graph state and returns updates. The first argument is always the state:

This node appends a message by concatenating in the return value (no reducer yet) and sets `extra_field`.

**Warning:** 
Nodes should return updates to the state directly, instead of mutating the state.

Define a simple graph with this node. Use [`StateGraph`](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#stategraph) for a graph that operates on this state, then [`add_node`](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#nodes) to populate the graph:

LangGraph provides built-in utilities for visualizing a graph. See [Visualize your graph](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-visualize) for detail.

```python
from IPython.display import Image, display

display(Image(graph.get_graph().draw_mermaid_png()))
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR

    classDef process fill:#E5F4FF,stroke:#006DDD,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710
    classDef terminal fill:#F2FAFF,stroke:#40668D,stroke-width:2px,color:#030710

    class startNode terminal
```

This graph executes a single node. Invoke it:

```
{'messages': [HumanMessage(content='Hi'), AIMessage(content='Hello!')], 'extra_field': 10}
```

Note that:

* Invocation started by updating a single key of the state.
* The invocation result includes the entire state.

Inspect [message](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/messages) content with pretty-print:

```

Hi
================================== Ai Message ==================================

Hello!
```

Define and update state > Process state updates with reducers

Each key in the state can have its own [reducer](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#reducers) function, which controls how updates from nodes are applied. If no reducer is specified, updates to that key replace the previous value.

For `TypedDict` state schemas, define reducers by annotating the field with a reducer function.

In the earlier example, the node updated `"messages"` by returning the full concatenated list. Add a reducer so updates are appended automatically:

The node can then return only the new message:

```
================================ Human Message ================================

Hi
================================== Ai Message ==================================

Hello!
```

Define and update state > Process state updates with reducers > MessagesState

In practice, lists of messages need more than plain concatenation:

* Update an existing message in the state by ID.
* Accept shorthand [message formats](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#serialization), such as `{"role": "user", "content": "..."}`.

LangGraph includes a built-in reducer @[`add_messages`] that handles these cases:

```
================================ Human Message ================================

Hi
================================== Ai Message ==================================

Hello!
```

This shape fits applications that use [chat models](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/models). For convenience, subclass the prebuilt `MessagesState`:

Define and update state > Resetting a reducer field

A common source of confusion with reducers is that with a merging reducer, returning an empty value does not clear the field. The reducer merges the right argument into the left one, so an empty update is merged in and previously accumulated values are kept.

This pattern matters for error buffers or retry counters that must be cleared between retry attempts:

To clear the field while keeping a merging reducer, wrap the update with [`Overwrite`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/types/):

For more information, see [Bypass reducers with Overwrite](#bypass-reducers-with-overwrite).

Define and update state > Bypass reducers with `Overwrite`

In some cases, you may want to bypass a reducer and directly overwrite a state value. When a node returns a value wrapped with `Overwrite`, the reducer is bypassed and the channel is set directly to that value.

This is useful when you want to reset or replace accumulated state rather than merge it with existing values.

LangGraph provides the [`Overwrite`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/types/) type for this purpose.

```
['replacement message']
```

You can also use JSON format with the special key `"__overwrite__"`:

**Warning:** 
When nodes execute in parallel, only one node can use `Overwrite` on the same state key in a given super-step. If multiple nodes attempt to overwrite the same key in the same super-step, an `InvalidUpdateError` will be raised. An `Overwrite` also discards regular updates that other nodes write to the same key in that super-step. The key ends up with only the `Overwrite` value.

Define and update state > Define input and output schemas

By default, `StateGraph` operates with a single schema, and all nodes communicate using that schema. You can also define distinct input and output schemas.

When distinct schemas are specified, an internal schema is still used for communication between nodes. The input schema validates the provided input. The output schema filters the internal data so `invoke` returns only the fields in the output schema.

Define distinct input and output schemas:

```
{'answer': 'bye'}
```

Notice that the output of invoke only includes the output schema.

Define and update state > Pass private state between nodes

Nodes sometimes need intermediate data that should not appear in the graph's main input or output schema. Keep that data private so only the nodes that need it can read it.

The following sequential graph has three nodes. Private data passes between the first two steps. The third step only sees the public overall state.

```
Entered node `node_1`:
    Input: {'a': 'set at start'}.
    Returned: {'private_data': 'set by node_1'}
Entered node `node_2`:
    Input: {'private_data': 'set by node_1'}.
    Returned: {'a': 'set by node_2'}
Entered node `node_3`:
    Input: {'a': 'set by node_2'}.
    Returned: {'a': 'set by node_3'}

Output of graph invocation: {'a': 'set by node_3'}
```

Define and update state > Private channels and streaming

Input, output, and private schemas constrain what each node reads and what `invoke` returns. They do **not** hide channels from [streaming](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming).

Values streaming emits **all** state channels by default, including private ones. That applies to the values projection from [event streaming](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/event-streaming) (`stream.values` on `stream_events` / `streamEvents` with `version="v3"`), and to `graph.stream` with `stream_mode="values"` / `streamMode: "values"`. Values streaming uses the full state, not the output schema. A private channel can be missing from `invoke` output but visible in the stream.

This example uses distinct input, output, overall, and private schemas. `invoke` returns only the output schema:

Streaming with the values projection still includes the private `bar` channel:

To restrict streamed values to specific channels (for example, only the output schema), pass `output_keys` to `graph.stream`:

If you only need the channels a node produced in each step (not the full accumulated state), use `stream_mode="updates"` instead. See [Streaming](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming).

Define and update state > Use pydantic models for graph state

A @[StateGraph] accepts a @[`state_schema`] argument that specifies the shape of the state nodes can access and update.

Most examples on this page use a Python-native `TypedDict` or [`dataclass`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html) for `state_schema`. @[`state_schema`] can be any [type](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#type-objects).

Use a [Pydantic BaseModel](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/base_model/) for @[`state_schema`] when you need runtime validation on **inputs**.

**Note:** 
**Known Limitations**
* The output of the graph is **not** an instance of a Pydantic model.
* Runtime validation only occurs on inputs to the first node in the graph, not on subsequent nodes or outputs.
* The validation error trace from Pydantic does not show which node the error arises in.
* Pydantic's recursive validation can be slow. For performance-sensitive applications, prefer a `dataclass`.

Invoke the graph with an **invalid** input

```
An exception was raised because `a` is an integer rather than a string.
1 validation error for OverallState
a
  Input should be a valid string [type=string_type, input_value=123, input_type=int]
    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.9/v/string_type
```

See below for additional features of Pydantic model state:

**Serialization Behavior**

  When using Pydantic models as state schemas, serialization matters especially when:

  * Passing Pydantic objects as inputs
  * Receiving outputs from the graph
  * Working with nested Pydantic models

  The following example shows these behaviors:

  

**Runtime Type Coercion**

  Pydantic performs runtime type coercion for certain data types. That can help, but it can also produce unexpected values if you do not account for it.

  

**Working with Message Models**

  When working with LangChain message types in a state schema, serialization matters. Use `AnyMessage` (rather than `BaseMessage`) for proper serialization and deserialization when message objects travel over the wire.

Visualize your graph
Render LangGraph graphs as Mermaid diagrams or PNG images for debugging and documentation.

Render a compiled graph as Mermaid text or a PNG image to inspect topology and debug routing. For an interactive UI, use [LangSmith Studio](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/studio) with a [local server](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/local-server).

You can visualize any compiled graph that exposes `get_graph()`, including @[`StateGraph`]. See the [Graph](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/graphs/) reference.

The examples below use the same small graph in both languages: two nodes, a conditional edge from `node1`, and a loop back from `node2`.

Visualize your graph > Mermaid Call `draw_mermaid()` on the drawable graph to get Mermaid syntax. Paste the string into any Mermaid renderer, or keep it in docs and PRs. ``` --- config: flowchart: curve: linear --- graph TD; __start__([

__start__

]):::first node1(node1) node2(node2) __end__([

__end__

]):::last __start__ --> node1; node1 -.-> __end__; node1 -.-> node2; node2 --> node1; classDef default fill:#f2f0ff,line-height:1.2 classDef first fill-opacity:0 classDef last fill:#bfb6fc ```

Graph API overview
Learn how LangGraph models agent workflows as graphs of shared state, nodes, and edges.

The Graph API defines agent workflows as a graph of [state](#state), [nodes](#nodes), and [edges](#edges). [`Send`](#send) and [`Command`](#command) control how the graph runs work: `Send` dynamically invokes nodes for fan-out, and `Command` updates state while routing to the next node (including resume after an interrupt). Use the Graph API when you want explicit shared state and a visual control flow.

For step-by-step decisions while building, see the [Build checklist for the Graph API](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/use-graph-api). For a guided walkthrough, see [Thinking in the Graph API](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/thinking-in-graph-api).

Graph API overview > Graphs

LangGraph models agent workflows as graphs built from three parts:

1. [`State`](#state): A shared snapshot of the application. Usually a typed schema.
2. [`Nodes`](#nodes): Functions that read state, do work, and return updates.
3. [`Edges`](#edges): Fixed or conditional transitions that determine the next node.

Compose nodes and edges to build sequences, branches, and loops. Nodes and edges are ordinary functions. They can call an LLM or run other code.

In short: nodes do the work; edges decide what runs next.

Graph API overview > Graphs > Super-steps

LangGraph runs graphs with [message passing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Message_passing), in the style of Google's [Pregel](https://research.google/pubs/pregel-a-system-for-large-scale-graph-processing/) system. Execution advances in discrete **super-steps**:

- Nodes that run in parallel share one super-step.
- Nodes that run in sequence use separate super-steps.
- A node becomes active when it receives input on an incoming edge.
- After a super-step, nodes with no pending messages become inactive.
- The run ends when every node is inactive and no messages remain in transit.

Graph API overview > Graphs > StateGraph

@[`StateGraph`] is the main graph builder. Parameterize it with your state schema.

Graph API overview > Graphs > Compiling your graph

Build a graph by defining [state](#state), adding [nodes](#nodes) and [edges](#edges), then compiling. Compilation checks the graph structure (for example for orphaned nodes). It is also where you attach runtime options such as [checkpointers](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence) and breakpoints.

You must compile the graph before you invoke or stream it. This is the smallest end-to-end example:

Graph API overview > State

State is the shared data that nodes read and update. LangGraph stores that data in **channels**: named slots in the state schema (the keys of your state object). Each channel holds a value and defines how updates merge into it. Most channels use last-write-wins. Channels with a [reducer](#reducers) combine values instead, for example by appending to a list.

State has two parts:

- A [schema](#schema) that declares the channels in the graph
- Optional [reducers](#reducers) that control how updates merge into each channel

Nodes return partial updates. LangGraph applies those updates through each channel's reducer.

Define state with a [`TypedDict`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.TypedDict), a [`dataclass`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html) (for defaults), or a Pydantic [`BaseModel`](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state#use-pydantic-models-for-graph-state) when you need validation. Prefer `TypedDict` or `dataclass` for performance.

**Info:** 
[`create_agent`](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/agents) state schemas must be `TypedDict`. Pydantic models are not supported.

Graph API overview > State > Schema

By default, the graph input and output schemas match the full state. You can narrow them when some keys are internal only. See [Define input and output schemas](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state#define-input-and-output-schemas).

#### Multiple schemas

Most graphs share one state schema. Use multiple schemas when you need either of the following:

- Private channels that internal nodes share, but that are not part of graph input or output
- Explicit input and output schemas that are subsets of the full internal state

A node can write to any channel in the graph state, including channels outside its declared input schema. Nodes can also introduce private channels when those schemas are defined. Input and output schemas constrain what `invoke` accepts and returns. They do not hide channels from [streaming](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/streaming) by default. See [Private channels and streaming](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state#private-channels-and-streaming).

For examples, see [Define input and output schemas](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state#define-input-and-output-schemas) and [Pass private state between nodes](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state#pass-private-state-between-nodes).

Graph API overview > State > Reducers

Reducers control how node updates merge into state. Each key has its own reducer. With no reducer, updates overwrite the previous value.

#### Reducer arguments

A reducer is a binary function:

- **Left**: The current value in state for that key
- **Right**: The update returned by a node for that key

```python
new_value = reducer(left=current_state[key], right=node_update[key])
```

Define a reducer and attach it to a state key with `Annotated`:

Calling the reducer with left and right shows how values combine:

#### Default reducer

The default reducer replaces the left value with the right. Nodes return partial updates, not the full state.

For example, start with `{"foo": 1, "bar": ["hi"]}`. An update of `{"foo": 2}` yields `{"foo": 2, "bar": ["hi"]}`. A later `{"bar": ["bye"]}` yields `{"foo": 2, "bar": ["bye"]}`.

#### Custom reducers

Use a custom reducer to combine values, such as appending to a list.

Here `foo` overwrites. `bar` appends with `operator.add`. From `{"foo": 1, "bar": ["hi"]}`, an update of `{"bar": ["bye"]}` becomes `{"foo": 1, "bar": ["hi", "bye"]}`.

#### Overwrite

To bypass a merging reducer and replace a value (including clearing it), use [`Overwrite`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/types/). See [Bypass reducers with Overwrite](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state#bypass-reducers-with-overwrite).

#### Resetting a reducer field

With a merging reducer, returning an empty value keeps prior data. That matters for error buffers or retry counters that must clear between attempts. See [Resetting a reducer field](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state#resetting-a-reducer-field) and [Bypass reducers with Overwrite](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api-state#bypass-reducers-with-overwrite).

Graph API overview > State > Working with messages in graph state

#### Why use messages?

Chat models take a list of messages as input. LangChain's [chat model interface](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/models) accepts message objects such as @[`HumanMessage`] and @[`AIMessage`]. See the [Messages conceptual guide](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/messages).

#### Using messages in your graph

Store conversation history as a list of messages in state, with a reducer that appends new messages and updates existing ones by ID.

Use @[`add_messages`] on a `messages` key. Plain `operator.add` only appends, so it cannot update an existing message in place during human-in-the-loop edits.

#### Serialization

Message reducers also deserialize common wire formats into LangChain message objects.

```python
# Supported
{"messages": [HumanMessage(content="message")]}

# Also supported
{"messages": [{"type": "human", "content": "message"}]}
```

Access attributes with dot notation, for example `state["messages"][-1].content`. See [LangChain serialization](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/messages#serialization).

#### MessagesState

`MessagesState` is a prebuilt state with a single `messages` key that uses @[`add_messages`]. Subclass it to add fields:

document:
Graph API overview > Nodes

Nodes are sync or async functions that implement a step of the graph.

A node can accept:

1. `state`: The graph [state](#state)
2. `config`: A @[`RunnableConfig`] with values such as `thread_id` and `tags`
3. `runtime`: A `Runtime` object with [runtime context](#runtime-context), `store`, `stream_writer`, `execution_info`, and related helpers

Add nodes with @[`add_node`]:

Behind the scenes, LangGraph wraps functions as @[`RunnableLambda`] so they gain batching, async support, and [tracing](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability).

If you omit a node name, LangGraph uses the function name.

Graph API overview > Nodes > Re-execution and idempotency

With a [checkpointer](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence), LangGraph saves checkpoints at [super-step](#super-steps) boundaries, not mid-function inside a node. After an [interrupt](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts) or [retry](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance#retries), the affected node runs again from the start of its function. Side effects before the pause run again.

Design node logic so re-execution is safe. Prefer idempotency keys, upserts, or read-before-write checks. For durable keys and external side effects under retries, see [Retry boundaries and idempotency](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance#retry-boundaries-and-idempotency). For effects around `interrupt()`, see [Side effects called before `interrupt` must be idempotent](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts#side-effects-called-before-interrupt-must-be-idempotent).

You can add or remove nodes and edges without breaking resume for existing threads. Resumed runs use saved state and the graph you compile now.

If a node calls [tasks](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/functional-api#task) or @[`interrupt`], stricter [determinism](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/functional-api#determinism) rules apply on resume. Completed task results are restored from the checkpointer. Changing task or interrupt order before the resume point can mismatch cached values. See [Idempotency](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/functional-api#idempotency).

Graph API overview > Nodes > Choose the unit of work

A [node](#nodes) is a checkpoint and retry boundary. It is also where the graph can take a different path. Deterministic work such as parsing, retrieval, or a fixed tool chain does not need its own node unless you want that boundary.

Ask whether the step decides what happens next, or executes something already decided. Then pick the primitive that matches the recovery behavior you need:

| Primitive | Own checkpoint | On resume or retry | Choose when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Plain function inside a node | No. It runs inside the node's [super-step](#super-steps). | Re-runs whenever the node re-runs. | No routing fork after the step, and repeating it with the rest of the node is acceptable. |
| [Task](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/functional-api#task) | No new graph checkpoint. The result is stored with the running entrypoint or parent checkpoint. | The enclosing entrypoint or node replays from the start. Completed tasks return stored results. | The step has a side effect or is expensive, and must not repeat on resume. |
| [Subgraph](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/use-subgraphs) | Yes for stateful modes: nodes checkpoint under a namespace of the parent thread. Compile with `checkpointer=False` for no subgraph checkpoints. | Stateful modes resume inside the subgraph at the interrupted or failed node. | The unit has its own routing or state schema, or more than one parent graph reuses it. |
| Graph node | Yes. A checkpoint follows the [super-step](#super-steps) it runs in. | Resume starts at that node. Earlier nodes do not re-run. | A routing fork is possible after the step, or you need an interrupt, resume, or [time travel](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/use-time-travel) boundary. |

For side effects under retries, see [Retry boundaries and idempotency](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance#retry-boundaries-and-idempotency). For task retries and timeouts, see [Fault tolerance](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/fault-tolerance).
